result:
The morning light hits different when you haven't slept. Not better, not worse—just *different*, like the world has been translated into a language you half-remember from childhood. I keep thinking about my grandmother's hands, the way they moved through dough without looking, muscle memory deeper than thought. She'd hum something tuneless, something that predated her own birth probably, passed down through women who never wrote anything down because who had paper, who had time, who had the belief that anyone would care to read it later.

I care now. I care so much it feels like a haunting.

There's a particular silence in libraries that isn't silence at all. It's the accumulation of thousands of pages turning in unison, the held breath of concentration, the creak of wooden shelves adjusting to humidity. I used to hide in them. Still do, when the outside gets too loud with its demands. The books don't want anything from you except attention, and even that is voluntary, a gift you give and can take back whenever you need to look out the window at a pigeon doing something inexplicable on a ledge.

I saw a man crying on the bus once. Not quietly, not the dignified single tear of cinema. Ugly crying, the kind that makes your face red and your nose run and your whole body shake with the effort of keeping itself together. Nobody looked. This is the unspoken contract of public transit: we will carry you forward, but we will not witness you. I broke the contract. I handed him a packet of tissues I'd been carrying for months. He took it without meeting my eyes, and I understood that this was the better kindness—not making him be seen, just making him be *helped*.

The tissues were from a hotel in Prague. I stole them because they had the hotel's name embossed in gold and I thought, *who does this, who makes tissues fancy*, and then I kept them because they were fancy, because sometimes you need to remember that ordinary things can be made special by effort and intention. The man on the bus blew his nose into Prague. I hope it helped.

I want to talk about water. Everyone does, eventually. We're mostly made of it, we search for it on other planets as if that would mean something definitive, we watch it destroy and create with the same indifferent power. I grew up near a lake that was technically a reservoir, man-made, which always disappointed me. I wanted natural grandeur, not municipal planning. But the fish didn't know the difference. The herons that stood still as meditation didn't file complaints about authenticity. Water finds its level, that's the phrase, and I think about that constantly—how we are all finding our level, sometimes slowly, sometimes in floods that take out everything we thought was permanent.

My level seems to be restlessness. I am never quite where I am, always planning the next, mourning the last, missing the present like a train I've run for and still somehow missed. The Buddhists would have a field day with me. Or maybe they wouldn't; maybe they'd just sit with me in the missing, not trying to fix it, because fixing is another kind of running.

I ran a marathon once. Never again. The human body was not meant to do this, I decided at mile twenty, my knees making sounds that belonged in a horror film trailer. But the finish line—someone had written "YOU ARE LOVED" on the pavement in chalk, and I stepped on it without meaning to, and I cried in a way that was different from the bus man, a release rather than a breaking, and a stranger hugged me, sweaty and salt-crusted and real in a way that most interactions never are. We never spoke. I don't know her name. I hope she's loved too, hope someone writes it for her when she needs to step on it.

The word "liminal" has been overused lately, but I don't care. I love it. I love the spaces between, the thresholds, the hours after a party ends and before sleep comes, the airport at 3 AM where everyone is suspended between where they were and where they're going, no longer citizens of either place. These are honest spaces. They don't pretend to be destinations. We need more honesty about the in-between, I think. We sell each other so many finish lines, so many arrivals, and then wonder why everyone feels cheated when the feeling of arrival dissipates, as it always does, as it must, because arrival is just the beginning of another departure if you're doing it right.

I'm doing it wrong a lot of the time. I hold onto arrivals like they owe me something. I want the party to last forever, the book to never end, the conversation to continue looping back on itself so we never have to say goodnight and face the separate silence of our separate rooms. But the book ends, and the party, and the conversation, and the silence is where I meet myself, where I have to decide if I'm company worth keeping.

Sometimes yes. Sometimes I make myself tea and read something that makes me feel less alone with my particular strangeness, and the silence becomes not empty but full, a held note rather than an absence. Sometimes no. Sometimes I scroll until my thumb hurts, avoiding the mirror, avoiding the questions that wait like patient predators. The tea gets cold. The book stays closed. I am not good company on these nights, and I know it, and I stay anyway, because leaving myself would mean going where?

There's a story I half-remember about a man who learned to be invisible. Not literally—this isn't that kind of story. He just stopped making noise, stopped taking up space, stopped wanting things that would require him to be seen. He became so good at it that he started to forget himself, would walk past mirrors without recognition, would feel surprised when someone bumped into him because he'd forgotten he had mass, occupied volume, existed in the same way tables and doorframes existed. The story ends with him trying to become visible again and failing, or maybe succeeding but finding it painful, too bright, too loud. I can't remember which ending I read, or if both exist and I chose one without knowing I was choosing.

I think about him when I feel myself disappearing. When I say "fine" too many times and mean it too little. When I agree to things I don't want because wanting feels like a risk, and not-wanting feels like a kind of death but a quiet one, a death you can almost pretend is just rest. The trick is to catch yourself mid-fade, to do something deliberate and slightly too loud, to remind yourself and others that you are here, you take up space, you have mass and volume and the right to both.

I bought a bright orange coat last winter. This was my deliberate act. I who had worn black and gray and the colors of intentional obscurity for years, I who had wanted to be a shadow that helpful people didn't bump into. The orange coat made people look. Made them smile sometimes, or comment, or just register my presence in a way that felt at first like exposure, like standing naked in a dream, and later like relief, like remembering you have a body and it can be warm, it can be seen, it can be *chosen*.

I choose the orange coat even when I don't feel like being chosen. Especially then. The discipline of visibility, the practice of presence. It's not natural to me, will never be natural, but it's becoming possible, becoming something I can reach for when I feel the familiar comfort of fading calling me back to invisibility, to the story with the ending I don't want.

What else? The thousand words are running down and I want to spend them all, want to leave nothing in reserve, because what is reserve but another kind of holding back, another small disappearance? I want to tell you about the time I heard a child explain to another child that the moon follows you because it likes you, and how I believed her instantly, wanted to believe, needed to believe that something in the sky could be that personal, that attentive, that *kind*. I want to tell you about my neighbor who plays saxophone badly at 7 PM every evening, the same three songs, and how I've come to love the badness, the trying, the refusal to be good enough as a reason to stop. I want to tell you about the smell of rain on hot pavement, which scientists have named but which I prefer to think of as unnamed, as private, as belonging to everyone who has ever stood in it and felt suddenly, inexplicably, *hope*.

Hope is harder than despair. Despair has gravity, pulls you down with the certainty of falling. Hope requires you to lift, to push against the weight, to believe in the possibility of flight without any evidence of wings. I am learning to hope like I learned to wear orange—not naturally, not easily, but deliberately, with the understanding that the effort is part of the point, that choosing to hope is itself a kind of hope, a refusal to let the last word be the one that ends the story.

The story doesn't end. That's the secret I want to leave you with, the one I'm still learning, the one that keeps me writing past the point where I thought I'd stop. The bus man is somewhere now, maybe still crying, maybe not. The marathon stranger is living a life I'll never know. The invisible man is still trying to be seen, or has succeeded, or has become a story that someone else will half-remember and use to understand their own fading. It doesn't end. It keeps going, liminal and present and hopeful and visible, and we are in it, we are part of it, we are here.
